text: So far, all the improvements you've made have happened offline.

You had a fixed set of cases, you changed the agent, and then you ran
the same cases again to see what improved and what regressed.

That gives you a controlled way to make changes before real users ever
see them. But once the agent is live, the environment changes.
Now people are going to ask things you didn't put in your test set.

They'll phrase familiar requests in unfamiliar ways,
they'll leave out context, combine several things into one message,
and sometimes behave in ways that are hard to anticipate in advance.

So after deployment, one of the most important questions becomes,
where do the next improvement targets come from?
Usually, they come from production. Think about the dog shelter agent.

Maybe your offline test set includes a volunteer saying,
"I have limited mobility,"

and the agent correctly recognizes that this matters when deciding
which dogs are appropriate.

But a real volunteer might say, "I can only walk
for about ten minutes."
The underlying constraint is similar, but the wording is different.

Or someone might ask, "Is Pepper free Saturday, and if not,
can I switch to Sunday?"

Now the agent has to handle availability and a fallback request
in the same message.
And some problems have nothing to do with the wording of the request.

Maybe the agent gives the right answer,
but it takes 14 seconds instead of 2.

Maybe a shelter policy changes, so behavior that was correct last
month is no longer correct today.

And what if a new kind of dog record appears with fields your original
benchmark never covered?

A good offline benchmark can catch a lot,
but it can only test the situations that made it into the benchmark.

That's why production becomes another source of evidence for
optimization. Your offline evals still have an important job.

They're where you can test a candidate change against known cases
in a repeatable way.
Before releasing a new version,

you can run it against the failures you wanted to improve
and the cases you want to protect from regression.

You can also automate those checks as part of your development
process, and for some applications,

you may decide that certain evals have to meet a threshold
before a release goes out.
The exact release rule depends on the product.

The important part is that offline evaluation gives you a stable place
to compare versions before the new behavior reaches users.
Production gives you something different.

It shows you what your benchmark missed, and there are several sources
of information you can use once the agent is live.

Let's go over four kinds of evidence that are commonly used.
production monitoring, manual review, user feedback, and A/B testing.

In production monitoring, you run evaluators and track metrics across
live traces to see where problems are appearing at scale.

Suppose a policy evaluator suddenly starts
flagging more conversations,

or a metric such as average tool use or response latency starts
creeping higher after a release.

Production monitoring will alert you to that kind of problem
and help you answer a key question: Where should I look?

Once you find an interesting issue, you often need to inspect the
traces themselves. That's where manual review comes in.
Imagine 37 shelter conversations fail an eligibility evaluator.

The count tells you there's a problem, but it doesn't tell you what
kind of problem. Open a few of those traces.

Did the agent skip the eligibility check?
Did it call the right tool with the wrong argument?
Did the lookup return the correct result, but the agent ignored it?

Or did the agent follow the right process and still reach
the wrong conclusion?

Reading the trace helps you turn a metric into a failure pattern you
can actually work on.

User feedback gives you another source of evidence.
Sometimes that's explicit, like a thumbs down or a complaint.
Sometimes it's behavioral.

A user asks the same question again and rephrases it three times,
then they abandon the conversation and ask to talk to a human agent.

None of those signals tells you exactly what failed on its own, but
they can point you towards interactions that deserve a closer look.

Once you have a candidate improvement, you may also want to compare
versions on real traffic. That's where an A/B test can be useful.

You can send some traffic to the current version and some to
the revised version,
then compare the outcomes that matter for your application.

The new version might help reduce policy failures or the amount of
follow-up turns users need to get to the outcome they're looking for.

Or it might lead the agent to answer just
as accurately but take longer.

The important thing is that these methods answer different questions.
Monitoring helps you find where something is happening.

Manual review helps you understand what happened. User feedback helps
surface problems that matter to the people using the system.

And A/B testing can help you see whether a change still looks
useful under real traffic.

You'll often use more than one of them on the same problem. There's
another thing production makes much more visible: operational cost.

Earlier, you saw this with the grounding rule you added to
the Northwind agent.

"Never state a product detail unless a tool result supports it."
Remember what happened?

You got rid of ungrounded answers, but the new rule caused the agent
to start making unnecessary tool calls.

At a small scale, one extra call may not look important.
But imagine that behavior repeating thousands of times a day.
You'll end up getting significantly more latency and cost.

The same is true for token use, model choice, repeated tool calls,
unnecessary handoffs,
or conversations where users have to keep asking for the same thing.

So when you monitor an agent in production,
don't look only at whether the answer was correct.

A useful system also has to behave efficiently enough for the
environment it runs in.

This is where the offline and production sides of the improvement
loop start to connect.

For the dog shelter agent, suppose production monitoring starts
flagging conversations where volunteers mention physical limitations.

You open one of those traces and see a volunteer say,
"I can only walk for about ten minutes. Is Pepper free on Saturday?"
The agent checks Pepper's availability and schedules the outing,

but it never considers whether Pepper is a suitable match for someone
who can only walk for ten minutes.

most likely because of a physical impairment.
Now you have a specific production failure.
Open the trace, and find the first place the behavior goes wrong.
In this case, the agent understood the scheduling request,

but it didn't recognize the walking time limit as information
that should affect the match.
Next, decide what the agent should have done instead.

It should have treated "I can only walk for about 10 minutes"
as a constraint on the kind of dog this volunteer can handle,

checked Pepper against that constraint,
and only then continued with scheduling.
Now, save that conversation as a new test case.

Keep the volunteer's original wording because that wording is part of
what your old test set was missing.

Record the behavior you expect and add the case to your
offline evaluation set.

Then, you can make a targeted change to the agent and run the updated
version against this new case. But don't run only this one.
Run the rest of your benchmark, too.
You still want the agent to handle the older mobility cases correctly,

and you don't want a change made for this new phrasing to break
scheduling requests that were already working.

If the new version now handles the 10-minute walking constraint
correctly and the rest of the benchmark stays healthy,
you have a stronger candidate to release.

Once that version is live, keep monitoring the same
kinds of conversations.

Maybe the next volunteer says, "I'm fine with short walks,
but nothing strenuous."

That may reveal another phrasing your offline set doesn't cover yet.
And when that happens, you do the same thing again.

inspect the trace, establish the expected behavior,
add the case to your benchmark, and use it to guide the next change.
That's how production starts feeding the offline eval set.

Each real failure you decide is worth fixing becomes a case the next
version has to handle too. That gives you a continuous loop.

Production reveals something your existing tests missed,
you inspect it and turn it into a reproducible case,

make a change and test it offline, then you release the new version
and see what real users show you next.

Over time, your benchmark becomes more representative of the
situations your agent actually encounters,

and your optimization process gets better, too, because each new
failure gives you another piece of evidence to work with.

In the next video, you'll follow that loop with
Northwind. See you there!
